subChunks.title: MVCC Dead Tuples, VACUUM, and AUTOVACUUM
subChunks.hookHtml: PostgreSQL's MVCC creates dead rows that accumulate over time. Without regular cleanup, tables bloat, queries slow, and XID wraparound can corrupt the entire database.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
How MVCC creates dead tuples

When a row is updated or deleted, PostgreSQL does not overwrite it. It marks the old version as dead (expired) and inserts a new version. The old version (dead tuple) remains in the table until cleaned up.

High-update tables accumulate thousands of dead tuples per second. Without cleanup, the physical table grows even if the logical row count stays constant.

VACUUM

-- Reclaim space from dead tuples (marks pages as reusable):
VACUUM apprentices;

-- Also updates statistics:
VACUUM ANALYZE apprentices;

-- Full rewrite (reclaims OS-level space — causes exclusive lock):
VACUUM FULL apprentices;  -- DANGER: locks the table, use sparingly

Regular VACUUM marks dead-tuple space as reusable within the table. It does NOT shrink the file on disk — VACUUM FULL does, but at the cost of an exclusive lock.

AUTOVACUUM

PostgreSQL runs autovacuum automatically based on table activity. The default threshold: vacuum when dead tuples exceed 20% + 50 rows of the live row count.

-- Check if autovacuum is keeping up:
SELECT relname, n_dead_tup, n_live_tup,
       last_autovacuum, last_autoanalyze
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC;

XID Wraparound — the most dangerous failure mode

PostgreSQL uses 32-bit transaction IDs (XIDs). After ~2 billion transactions, the XID wraps around and old transactions could appear to be in the future — corrupting the entire database. VACUUM prevents this by advancing the frozen XID floor.

-- Check for wraparound risk:
SELECT datname, age(datfrozenxid) AS xid_age
FROM pg_database
ORDER BY xid_age DESC;
-- DANGER threshold: age > 1.5 billion

Table bloat causes

  • High-update tables: UPDATE XP on 10M apprentices = 10M dead tuples/day
  • Long-running transactions: hold back the visibility horizon, preventing VACUUM from cleaning
  • Replication slots with lag: hold WAL, delay VACUUM

storyBeats.text: The apprentices table is 200GB but contains only 50M rows — each row averages 20 bytes. Something is wrong.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: MVCC never overwrites. Every update creates a new version; the old version stays as a dead tuple until VACUUM arrives. If VACUUM cannot keep up — or a long transaction holds the visibility horizon — dead tuples accumulate. The table grows. Queries slow. And XID wraparound, left unaddressed for long enough, will corrupt the entire archive.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Bloat diagnosis

Interpret this pg_stat_user_tables output and recommend action:

relname        | n_live_tup | n_dead_tup | last_autovacuum
---------------+------------+------------+-----------------
apprentices    | 50,000,000 | 18,000,000 | 3 hours ago
quest_completions | 2,000,000 | 1,800,000 | 2 days ago
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
apprentices: 18M dead tuples on 50M live (36%) — above the 20% autovacuum threshold. Autovacuum ran 3 hours ago — it may be running but not keeping up with write volume. Immediate actions:
1. Manually run: VACUUM ANALYZE apprentices; to catch up
2. Tune autovacuum for this table: ALTER TABLE apprentices SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.05) to trigger more frequently
3. Check for long-running transactions blocking VACUUM: SELECT pid, now() - xact_start FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state != 'idle' AND xact_start IS NOT NULL

quest_completions: 1.8M dead out of 2M live (90%) — severely bloated. Last autovacuum was 2 days ago — autovacuum is not running for this table. This is serious. Actions:
1. Run VACUUM ANALYZE quest_completions immediately
2. Investigate why autovacuum is not running (connection limit, locks, autovacuum_enabled = false?)
3. If table cannot be vacuumed due to locks: find and kill the blocking long transaction
4. Monitor XID age: SELECT age(datfrozenxid) FROM pg_database WHERE datname = current_database();
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo

Explain XID wraparound: what it is, why it is dangerous, and what PostgreSQL does to prevent it. What does the age(datfrozenxid) metric tell you?
subChunks.modelAnswer:
XID wraparound: PostgreSQL uses 32-bit transaction IDs (XIDs) that cycle from 0 to 2^31 (about 2.1 billion). The XID space is split: the past half and the future half. When transactions advance past the midpoint, old transactions fall into the 'future' half — PostgreSQL would think they haven't happened yet. This corrupts visibility calculations and can make all data appear invisible.

Danger: if you run 2+ billion transactions without vacuuming, the oldest unfrozen XID falls into the 'future' — PostgreSQL goes into safety shutdown ('database is not accepting commands to avoid wraparound data loss') or silently corrupts data.

Prevention: VACUUM freezes old tuples by replacing their XID with a special FrozenTransactionId that is always considered past. Autovacuum aggressively vacuums tables as they approach the wraparound age.

age(datfrozenxid): reports how many transactions ago the database last froze all tuples. At 200M it is fine. At 1.5B you should be concerned and investigate. At 2.1B you are in immediate danger.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain what dead tuples are, why they accumulate, and how VACUUM addresses them. Why is VACUUM FULL dangerous on a live production table?

questions.prompt: Why does PostgreSQL leave 'dead tuples' after an UPDATE?
options: MVCC keeps old row versions so other transactions can still see the old state — dead tuples are cleaned by VACUUM later
PostgreSQL does not delete rows immediately for performance
Dead tuples are a backup mechanism
Dead tuples are indexes that were not updated
questions.answer: MVCC keeps old row versions so other transactions can still see the old state — dead tuples are cleaned by VACUUM later
questions.explanation: MVCC creates a new row version on UPDATE and marks the old one as deleted. Other transactions that started before the UPDATE still see the old version. Once no transaction needs the old version, VACUUM marks it as reclaimable.

questions.prompt: What does VACUUM (without FULL) actually do?
options: Marks dead tuple space as reusable within the table — does not shrink the physical file
Deletes all dead tuples and compacts the file
Rewrites the entire table to reclaim OS-level disk space
questions.answer: Marks dead tuple space as reusable within the table — does not shrink the physical file
questions.explanation: Regular VACUUM marks dead-tuple pages as available for new data. The file stays the same size on disk — it just fills dead pages with new rows. VACUUM FULL rewrites the entire table, shrinking the file, but requires an exclusive lock.

questions.prompt: A long-running transaction (open for 3 hours) is preventing VACUUM from cleaning dead tuples. Why?
options: VACUUM cannot remove rows that might still be visible to the oldest active transaction — the long transaction holds the visibility horizon
Long transactions acquire a table lock that blocks VACUUM
VACUUM requires exclusive access to remove dead tuples
The long transaction is writing to the table, preventing VACUUM from reading it
questions.answer: VACUUM cannot remove rows that might still be visible to the oldest active transaction — the long transaction holds the visibility horizon
questions.explanation: VACUUM can only remove dead tuples that are invisible to all currently open transactions. A long transaction that started hours ago might still need to see those old row versions. VACUUM skips them until the blocking transaction ends.

questions.prompt: age(datfrozenxid) for the production database is 1.8 billion. What should you do?
options: Immediately run VACUUM FREEZE on the largest tables and investigate why autovacuum is not keeping up — 1.8B is dangerously close to the 2.1B wraparound limit
Increase max_connections to give autovacuum more resources
Restart the database to reset the XID counter
questions.answer: Immediately run VACUUM FREEZE on the largest tables and investigate why autovacuum is not keeping up — 1.8B is dangerously close to the 2.1B wraparound limit
questions.explanation: 1.8B is ~300M transactions from wraparound. At 1000 transactions/second that is ~3.5 days. This is a production emergency. Run VACUUM FREEZE aggressively. Find and kill any blocking long transactions. Review autovacuum settings and logs. Do not wait.
